title: BMO Deploys Agentic AI to Resolve Card Issues Faster
summary: BMO launched agentic AI technology to autonomously resolve credit and debit card problems, cutting resolution times and improving customer experience.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- BMO launched an agentic AI system on November 6, 2026 to autonomously handle credit and debit card issues without human intervention.
- The AI agents diagnose problems, execute fixes, and communicate resolutions directly to customers, reducing average resolution times significantly.
- This deployment represents one of the first large-scale banking implementations of fully autonomous AI agents in customer service operations.


BMO Financial Group deployed an[agentic AI](https://emergent.sh/glossary/what-is-agentic-ai) platform to autonomously resolve credit and debit card issues for customers, marking a significant shift in how major banks handle routine support operations. The system, which went live across BMO's North American operations, can independently diagnose card problems, execute fixes, and communicate resolutions without requiring human intervention at any step of the process.


## How the Agentic AI System Works


The platform uses autonomous agents that can access multiple banking systems simultaneously, cross-reference transaction data, identify root causes of card declines or fraud alerts, and implement corrections in real time. According to BMO's infrastructure team, the agents handle tasks that previously required 15-20 minutes of human analyst time per case, now resolving most standard issues in under two minutes.


Each agent operates within defined guardrails that prevent unauthorized account changes while still allowing broad decision-making authority for common scenarios like disputed charges, card activation failures, and temporary holds triggered by unusual spending patterns. The system reportedly processes natural language requests from customers through chat, email, and voice channels, then translates those inputs into executable banking operations.


## Officially Launched on November 6, 2026


BMO confirmed the system went into full production on November 6, 2026 after a six-month internal pilot program involving 50,000 customer interactions. The bank has not disclosed which AI vendor powers the underlying large language model, but banking technology analysts suggest the implementation likely combines foundation models with proprietary banking logic layers developed in-house.


The deployment covers all personal and small business banking customers across Canada and the United States, representing approximately 12 million active card accounts. BMO plans to expand the agentic capabilities to other service areas, including account opening processes and loan application reviews, later in 2026.


## Impact on Customer Service Operations


Early internal metrics show the agentic AI handles 65% of card-related inquiries end-to-end without escalation, a rate BMO expects to rise as the agents learn from edge cases. Human specialists now focus on complex disputes and regulatory compliance reviews rather than routine troubleshooting.


- Average resolution time dropped from 18 minutes to under 2 minutes for standard card issues
- Customer satisfaction scores improved by 12 percentage points in pilot groups
- After-hours support capacity increased 300% without adding staff


The bank has reassigned approximately 200 customer service representatives to higher-value roles, including fraud investigation and relationship management, rather than conducting layoffs. This approach reflects broader industry trends toward augmentation rather than replacement as banks adopt AI agents.


## What This Means for Banking Automation


BMO's deployment signals accelerating confidence in agentic AI for regulated financial operations. Unlike earlier chatbots that could only provide information, these agents execute transactions and modify account states, responsibilities that banks historically restricted to trained human employees. The success or failure of this implementation will likely influence how quickly competitors adopt similar systems, particularly as regulators develop frameworks for algorithmic accountability in consumer finance. For customers, the shift means faster resolutions for routine problems but raises questions about transparency when AI systems make consequential decisions about account access and dispute outcomes.
